715.title: Ghazals of longing
715.hook: his Persian love-poems to the Divine are still sung in gurdwaras
715.howItsDone: Ragis sing Bhai Nand Lal's Persian ghazals in kirtan in gurdwaras, alongside the Guru's bani, and Sikhs also read them in Persian and in translation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zindagi Nama, and your line, see him everywhere. What ordinary thing did you look at with longing? Day seven hundred fifteen.

In a gurdwara, the ragis sit with harmonium and tabla, and sing the Guru's own word from the Guru Granth Sahib. Then, now and then, the words change color. The language turns Persian. The tune softens. And the song is a love song, sung to God, by someone who sounds as if he can hardly bear the distance. Those songs were written by the poet we met two days ago. Today's word: ghazal.
screen: `RAGIS, HARMONIUM, TABLA.` → `THE WORDS CHANGE COLOR.` → `A LOVE SONG, SUNG TO GOD.`

segments.voice: A ghazal is a love poem with a shape of its own. The form began in Arabic and flowered in Persian. It's built from couplets, pairs of lines, and each couplet is complete in itself, like a bead. String the beads together and you have the ghazal. By custom, the poet signs the poem near the end, slipping his pen name into the last couplet. So in Bhai Nand Lal's ghazals, you'll hear him name himself: Goya. His ghazals are gathered in a collection known as the Divan-e-Goya. And what are they about? Longing. The lover and the Beloved. The ache of distance, the sweetness of a glance, the lover who would give anything for one meeting. That's the old language of the Persian ghazal, and Nand Lal draws on it. But in his poems the Beloved is the Divine, and the face the heart turns toward is the One, seen through the Guru. Hold three things together. First, the form. Each couplet stands alone, so a ragi can sing one, or several, and each still makes sense. A ghazal is easy to carry in pieces. Second, the feeling. Some people picture devotion as duty, a list of things to do. Nand Lal's ghazals sound more like someone who's simply in love, and can't hide it. Third, the place. These Persian love-songs aren't kept on a library shelf. They're sung in gurdwaras, in kirtan, in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikh custom welcomes them there. So a Persian love form found a home in the Guru's house, and it came in singing about love.
screen: `COUPLETS, EACH COMPLETE.` · `THE POET SIGNS: GOYA.` · `THE BELOVED IS THE DIVINE.` · `SUNG IN THE GURDWARA.` · then, large: `LOVE, IN PERSIAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one ghazal. If you can, find a recording of a ghazal of Bhai Nand Lal sung in kirtan, and play just a few minutes of it during the sit. If you can't, sit with the idea of one: a single couplet, complete in itself, sung slowly to someone you love. Don't try to understand every word. Let the sound do its work. Notice where the music lifts, and where it waits. If you pray, you can let Waheguru rise in you along with the tune. The bell holds the time.
Ghazal. A love poem built from couplets, as Persian poets shaped it, signed with the poet's pen name. Bhai Nand Lal's ghazals, signed Goya, are love songs to the Divine.
Your line: love, in persian. Today, hum one line of a song you love as if it were addressed to the One, and notice how it changes. Day seven hundred fifteen.

716.title: Rehat words
716.hook: writings on Sikh conduct are attributed to Nand Lal; historians discuss when they were set down
716.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada is the code of conduct agreed by the Panth today, and the older rahitnamas, including those attributed to Nand Lal, are studied as part of its background.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghazal, and your line, love, in persian. Did you hum a line as if it were addressed to the One? Day seven hundred sixteen.

Yesterday Nand Lal was a lover, singing in Persian. Today his name turns up somewhere quite different: on short writings about how a Sikh should live. Not love songs. Rules. What to do, what not to do, what a Sikh of the Guru keeps. It's a sudden change of tone, from the beloved's face to the kitchen table of daily life, and it comes with a puzzle about where those writings came from. Today: rehat words.
screen: `FROM LOVE SONGS TO RULES.` → `HOW A SIKH SHOULD LIVE.` → `A PUZZLE ABOUT THEIR ORIGIN.`

segments.voice: Rehat is the Sikh word for a way of living: conduct, discipline, the shape of a life. Writings that set it out are called rahitnamas. Some of them carry Nand Lal's name. One is often called the Tankhahnama, and another is a set of questions and answers. They're framed as a conversation: Nand Lal asks, and Guru Gobind Singh answers. What does a Sikh of the Guru do? What should a Sikh avoid? What's the fault, and how is it put right? And the answers are practical. They speak of things like joining the sangat, remembering the Name, honest dealing, and how a Sikh behaves toward the Guru's word and toward others. Now the puzzle, and here the honest thing is to say it plainly. These writings are attributed to Nand Lal. Historians discuss when they were actually set down, and whether everything in them comes from his own hand, or was written or added later and given his name. Sikh scholars and historians don't all read the evidence the same way. That's not a scandal. It's what can happen to old writing that people treasure: it's copied, recited, and handed down, and the question of who wrote which line gets complicated. Today, Sikhs keep an agreed code of conduct, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, and it's its own document. The rahitnamas are part of the long conversation behind it. Here's what's worth keeping, whatever the dates. The same name that signs love songs to God is attached to rules about daily life. In these writings, the two sit side by side: longing for the Beloved, and a discipline kept day by day.
screen: `REHAT: A WAY OF LIVING.` · `NAND LAL ASKS, THE GURU ANSWERS.` · `HISTORIANS DISCUSS THE DATES.` · `LOVE AND DISCIPLINE, ONE PATH.` · then, large: `A RULE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one rule of your own. Not a list. One. Use the sit to find it. Something small that would make your days more like the life you want. No phone at the table. A kind word before a hard one. Ten minutes of quiet before work. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence. Then picture keeping it today, and tomorrow, at the moment it'll be hardest. If you pray, you can hold that rule up as a small offering. The bell holds the time.
Rehat words. Writings on Sikh conduct, set out as Nand Lal asking and the Guru answering, attributed to him, with historians still discussing when they were set down.
Your line: a rule kept. Today, keep the one rule you chose, once, on purpose, even when nobody would notice. Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: Nand Lal's kitchen
717.hook: tradition says the Guru praised Nand Lal's langar above others because it served everyone, anytime
717.howItsDone: Gurdwara langars serve free food to anyone who comes, and Sikhs retell the story of Bhai Nand Lal's kitchen as a picture of a langar that never turns anyone away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rehat words, and your line, a rule kept. Did the one rule you chose for yourself hold for a whole day? Day seven hundred seventeen.

The dinner rush is over. Chairs are up on the tables, the floor is wet, the cook is wiping down the last pan. A traveler knocks on the glass. Kitchen's closed, someone mouths, and points at the sign with the opening hours. Nobody is being cruel. Hours are hours. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a kitchen that had no such sign. It belonged to the Persian poet we met a few days ago, the one who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court. Today: langar.
screen: `THE CHAIRS ARE UP ON THE TABLES.` → `KITCHEN'S CLOSED.` → `A KITCHEN WITH NO SIGN.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as it's usually told, and it comes to us as a sakhi, a story passed on, not from Nand Lal's own poems. At Anandpur, tradition says, several Sikhs ran langars, free kitchens. The Guru wanted to see what those kitchens were really like, so he went round them dressed as an ordinary traveler, at an hour when no meal was being served. At one door he was told to come back later. At another, the food wasn't ready, so there was nothing to give. Then he came to Nand Lal's kitchen. There, whatever was in the pots, finished or not, was put in front of him straight away. Later, the story goes, the Guru praised Nand Lal's langar above the others. Not because the food was finer. Because it served everyone, anytime. There's more than one thing folded into that. First, hunger doesn't keep office hours. A person who arrives late is exactly as hungry as one who arrives on time. Second, the other kitchens weren't wicked. They were organized. The story isn't against good planning; it's about what happens when the plan becomes a reason to send someone away. Third, notice what Nand Lal didn't wait for. He didn't wait for the meal to be perfect. He gave what there was, as it was. And last, notice who the traveler turned out to be. In Sikh telling, the one you serve at the odd hour may be the Guru himself, and the langar is set up so that it never needs to check. It's the same idea a gurdwara langar keeps today: food for whoever walks in, without asking who they are.
screen: `THE GURU GOES ROUND IN DISGUISE.` · `COME BACK LATER. NOTHING READY.` · `NAND LAL SERVES WHAT THERE IS.` · `HUNGER KEEPS NO OFFICE HOURS.` · then, large: `SERVE ANYTIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone unexpected. Use the sit to plan it. Who might turn up hungry today, outside the usual hours? A roommate coming in late. A coworker who skipped lunch. A neighbor, a delivery driver, someone on the corner you pass every morning. Choose one. Then choose what you already have: a piece of fruit, a sandwich, tea, leftovers, as they are. No need for it to be finished or fancy. Picture handing it over without asking anything first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture it. The bell holds the time.
Langar, the free kitchen that, in the story, fed a stranger at the wrong hour with whatever was in the pots, and was praised for it.
Your line: serve anytime. Today, when someone needs something at an inconvenient moment, give what you have, as it is. Day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: Sung in the gurdwara
718.hook: the Rehat Maryada allows only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal for kirtan
718.tomorrow: Reading a pauri of Bhai Gurdas
718.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis sing kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib, and at times sing a var of Bhai Gurdas or a ghazal of Bhai Nand Lal, the two writers the Sikh Rehat Maryada allows alongside Gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar, and your line, serve anytime. Did someone turn up at the wrong hour, and did you give what you had? Day seven hundred eighteen.

A line sung on Sunday turns up again on Tuesday, at the sink, or halfway through the drive to work. Words that are sung over and over don't stay in the room where they were sung. That makes a plain question matter in a gurdwara: which words get to be sung there? Plenty of poems have been written about the Gurus. The Sikh code of conduct gives a short, clear answer, and two names from this block are in it. Today: Rehat Maryada.
screen: `A LINE SUNG ON SUNDAY, HUMMED ON TUESDAY.` → `SUNG WORDS TRAVEL.` → `WHICH WORDS GET TO BE SUNG?`

segments.voice: The code is the Sikh Rehat Maryada, the document of Sikh conduct published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. In its section on kirtan, it says that in the congregation, only Gurbani, the Guru's own hymns, may be sung, along with the compositions that explain it: the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. That's the whole list, and it's short. Other poems have been written about the Gurus, many of them beautiful. The code doesn't call them bad. It simply keeps them out of kirtan in the sangat. Now look at how it describes the two poets. Not as extra scripture standing beside the Guru, but as a key to it. Their words are allowed because they help open the Gurbani. Bhai Gurdas, the scribe, with his vars full of pictures: the sun rising and the stars going out, the cup of milk at Multan. Bhai Nand Lal, the poet at Guru Gobind Singh's court, with his Persian ghazals of longing. One wrote in Punjabi and Braj, the other in Persian. Very different voices, both in. So when you sit in a gurdwara and the ragis start a piece, they sing Gurbani: in the code's own terms, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib and the hymns of Guru Gobind Singh. Sometimes, though, the ragi will announce that a var of Bhai Gurdas or a ghazal of Bhai Nand Lal is coming. That's the code at work: the Guru's word at the center, and two trusted servants allowed to stand nearby and explain it. Some readers hear in this a lesson about anything sung over and over: what gets repeated becomes part of the one who repeats it.
screen: `THE SIKH REHAT MARYADA ON KIRTAN.` · `GURBANI, AND TWO WHO EXPLAIN IT.` · `A SCRIBE AND A PERSIAN POET.` · `LISTEN FOR THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `THE TWO VOICES ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for their names in kirtan. That's for the next time you hear kirtan, in a gurdwara or on a stream: listen for the few words a ragi says before a piece begins, and whether Bhai Gurdas or Bhai Nand Lal is named. For now, use the sit to practice that kind of listening. Let the sounds around you come in: the fridge, the street, a voice in another room. Notice which ones you'd let in on purpose and which just arrive. Then ask: what words do I repeat most often in a day? The bell holds the time.
Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct that allows Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal in kirtan because they explain it.
Your line: the two voices allowed. Today, notice the songs and lines you repeat without thinking, and pick one you'd keep on purpose. Day seven hundred eighteen.

719.title: Reading a pauri of Bhai Gurdas
719.hook: a slow reading of one pauri, its picture, its point
719.howItsDone: In katha, a teacher in the gurdwara takes one pauri of Bhai Gurdas, describes its picture, and draws out its point for the sangat, often alongside a line of Gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehat Maryada, and your line, the two voices allowed. Which line did you decide to keep on purpose? Day seven hundred nineteen.

A forest. Tall trees, thick undergrowth, a bamboo grove rattling in the wind. And somewhere in the middle, one sandalwood tree. That's the whole opening of the stanza we're reading today. No hero, no journey, no miracle. Just trees standing next to each other. For days now we've heard about Bhai Gurdas and his vars. Today we stop talking about him and read him slowly, the way a ragi or a katha teacher would. Today: pauri.
screen: `A FOREST, A BAMBOO GROVE.` → `ONE SANDALWOOD TREE.` → `TODAY, WE READ HIM SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: A pauri is one stanza of a var, and Bhai Gurdas often builds his around a picture you could find in any village. So read in three steps. Step one: the picture. Let it stand before you look for meaning. A sandalwood tree grows in the forest, and its fragrance spreads. The trees around it, ordinary trees, pick up its scent. That's all. Stay with it. Step two: the twist. Bhai Gurdas pictures one tree that doesn't take the scent: the bamboo, standing right there beside the sandalwood. It's tall. It's hollow. Some readers hear pride in it: so taken up with its own height that the fragrance never gets in. Now the picture has tension. Closeness alone didn't change it. Step three: the point. For Bhai Gurdas, the sandalwood is the Guru, or the company of the Guru's Sikhs, the sangat. Ordinary people sitting near it take on something of its fragrance. But a person can sit right beside it, every week, and stay exactly the same, if they're hollow and puffed up with themselves. The pauri doesn't scold. It just shows you the bamboo and lets you notice it. That's the method. One picture, held long enough to see it. One twist that gives it an edge. One point, which the picture has already made before anyone states it.
screen: `STEP ONE: THE PICTURE.` · `STEP TWO: THE BAMBOO THAT STAYS THE SAME.` · `STEP THREE: THE POINT, THE SANGAT.` · `LET THE PICTURE MAKE THE POINT.` · then, large: `ONE PICTURE, ONE POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one pauri slowly. Today's will do. Close your eyes and build the picture first: the forest, the sandalwood, the ordinary trees around it slowly taking on its scent. Stay with the picture for the first part of the sit, without asking what it means. Then bring in the bamboo, tall and hollow, right beside it. Notice it. Only near the end, let the point arrive on its own. Where in your life are you sitting close to something good? If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly at the end. The bell holds the time.
Pauri, one stanza of a var, read first for its picture, then its twist, then the point that comes out of the picture itself.
Your line: one picture, one point. Today, when something strikes you, hold the picture before you decide what it means. Day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: Why tellers matter
720.hook: a story lives because someone tells it well and truly
720.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, katha is the spoken explanation of Gurbani: a teacher takes a line and opens it with stories, often drawing on Bhai Gurdas and the sakhis of the Gurus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri, and your line, one picture, one point. Did you hold a picture long enough to let it speak? Day seven hundred twenty.

A grandmother at the end of a family dinner, telling how she came to this country. The grandkids have heard it before. One of them corrects a detail. She waves it off and keeps going. Years later, she's gone, and that grandkid is the one at the end of the table, telling it to the next lot. Some details are different now. Is it still her story? Whether a story survives depends less on the story than on the people who keep telling it. Today: katha.
screen: `A STORY AT THE END OF DINNER.` → `THE GRANDKID TELLS IT NEXT.` → `IS IT STILL HER STORY?`

segments.voice: Sikhs have a word for the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani in the gurdwara: katha. A katha teacher sits before the sangat, takes a line, and opens it up with stories and pictures. Bhai Gurdas did a version of that in verse. His vars carry the Guru's teaching in the language of the fields and the bazaar, so people could hold on to it. Bhai Nand Lal did it in Persian, for listeners who loved that kind of poetry. That's why this block has called them tellers. Now, two words carry today's lesson: well and truly. They pull in different directions, and a good teller holds both. Well means the story has to land. If nobody can follow it, it dies with the teller. Yesterday's sandalwood and bamboo is told well: a picture that stays with you. Truly means the teller doesn't bend the story to make himself look good, or to win an argument. And here's the honest part: telling well can tempt you away from telling truly. A detail gets bigger with each retelling because it gets a better reaction. That's exactly why, starting next week, this path reads the janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, carefully. Different tellers told them differently, and the Sikhs who kept them have had to think about which tellings to trust. One more thing. Every Sikh who explains the Guru's teaching to a child, at a kitchen table, is a teller too. The chain didn't stop with Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. It runs through any household that passes the stories on.
screen: `KATHA: THE TELLING IN THE GURDWARA.` · `WELL: THE STORY HAS TO LAND.` · `TRULY: DON'T BEND IT.` · `EVERY HOUSEHOLD IS A TELLER.` · then, large: `TELL IT TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one story truly. Use the sit to choose a story you've told more than once. Something from your family, your work, something that happened to you. Run it through in your head the way you usually tell it. Then run it again and listen for the places where it's grown: the bit you've made a little funnier, a little bigger, a little kinder to yourself. You don't need to fix it right now. Just notice where the true version is. Later today, if the story comes up, tell that one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Katha, the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani in the gurdwara, kept alive and true the way Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal told it.
Your line: tell it true. Today, when you pass a story on, keep it as big as it really was, and no bigger. Day seven hundred twenty.

721.title: The tellers close
721.hook: a scribe and a poet, both servants of the Word
721.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal as companions to Gurbani; the Sikh code of conduct allows them in kirtan because they explain the Guru's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, katha, and your line, tell it true. Did a story come up, and did you keep it the size it really was? Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Two men who never needed to meet to belong together. One is bent over a page, pen in hand, writing out the Guru's hymns as Guru Arjan dictates, tradition says, and adding nothing of his own. The other sits at Guru Gobind Singh's court, writing Persian verses of longing for the Beloved. A careful hand and a burning heart. Different languages, different generations, different gifts. This block began with the first of them, and today it closes with both. Today: Shabad.
screen: `A PEN WRITING OUT THE HYMNS.` → `PERSIAN VERSES AT COURT.` → `A CAREFUL HAND, A BURNING HEART.`

segments.voice: Let's walk back through what the two of them gave us. Bhai Gurdas first. The scribe of the Granth, tradition says, who kept his own vars beside the book and never inside it. In his vars he told the world before Nanak, and the mist clearing when Nanak came. The debate at Achal, the cup of milk at Multan with the jasmine flower floating on it. The Guru bowing to his disciple. A roll of honor, ordinary Sikhs remembered by name and town. A Sikh's day from early rising to honest work. One Sikh, two a sangat, five where the Lord is present. Then Bhai Nand Lal. The Persian poet at Guru Gobind Singh's court. His book of life, longing to see the Beloved in everything. His ghazals, still sung. The rehat writings attributed to him, which historians discuss. And this week, the story of his kitchen, where the stranger was fed at the wrong hour. Now notice what joins them. Neither tried to become the Guru's rival. Bhai Gurdas wrote out the Guru's word and kept his own off the page. Nand Lal poured his gifts into praise. That's why the Sikh code of conduct lets their words be sung beside Gurbani: because they explain it, not replace it. They were servants of the Word, and the Word here means the Guru's word, the Shabad. And a servant here doesn't mean small. Both were gifted men, and their whole skill went into making the Guru's word clearer for someone else. Next week, the stories of Nanak's own life, the janamsakhis. Different tellers, different tellings. These two make a good pair to hold the new tellers beside.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teller in your life. Use the sit to bring one to mind. Someone who passed something good on to you: a grandparent with stories, a teacher who made a hard thing clear, a friend who first explained what a gurdwara was, the person who taught you a recipe or a prayer or a song. Hold their face for a moment. Remember one thing they told you, in their words if you can. Then plan how you'll thank them today: a message, a call, or, if they're gone, saying their name aloud. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
